Where it began

Yashpal Sharma was born in Ludhiana on 11 August 1954. People first took notice when he made 260 for Punjab schools against Jammu and Kashmir schools in 1972, and within two years he was playing for his state. An innings of 173 for North Zone in the Duleep Trophy, against a South Zone attack full of famous spinners, showed he could handle the best.

His nephew Chetan Sharma went on to play the game too, so cricket ran in the family.

The player

A score of 99 in the Irani Trophy took him on India's 1978 tour of Pakistan, where he played his first one-day international. His Test debut came at Lord's in August 1979, after a tour of England in which he made 884 runs in the other matches. He played 37 Tests from 1979 to 1983, making 1,606 runs at 33.46 with two hundreds and nine fifties.

The bigger of those hundreds was 140 against England at Madras in 1981–82. He batted through the whole of the second day with Gundappa Viswanath, and the pair added 316 for the third wicket. A year later at Port of Spain he was hit on the head by Malcolm Marshall, went off, and came back in the same innings to make a fifty.

What made him special

Sunil Gavaskar called him India's Crisis Man, and the name fitted. In the first match of the 1983 World Cup he top-scored with 89 as India handed the West Indies their first ever World Cup defeat, taking a fair few blows from Marshall along the way. In the semi-final against England he top-scored again, with 61, including a flick for six over square leg off a near-yorker from Bob Willis, a shot long remembered. Only one Indian made more runs in that triumphant campaign.

When the bowling was quickest and the stakes highest, he was usually the man in the middle holding things together.

Away from the middle

He kept playing domestic cricket for Punjab, Haryana and Railways, and at 37 he made hundreds in consecutive matches. He later stood as an umpire for a while, coached Uttar Pradesh and served twice as a national selector, the second time from 2008 to 2011, a spell that ended with India winning the 2011 World Cup. The 2021 film 83 told the story of that first World Cup win, with Jatin Sarna playing him.

He died in 2021, aged 66.

And finally

Playing for North Zone against the touring West Indies at Amritsar, he once hit Viv Richards for four sixes in a row. It is not often anyone got the better of Viv Richards, and almost never for four balls running.
